# More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents

Ruhan Wang    Kishan Panaganti    Dongruo Zhou Affiliation: \[
Affiliation: \[ Email: [ruhwang@iu.edu](mailto:) Email:
[kpb@global.tencent.com](mailto:) Email: [dz13@iu.edu](mailto:)

October 19, 2026

###### Abstract

LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by
storing experience from their own executions in external memory and
reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is
whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the
rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. Retaining these
abstractions allows agents to reuse strategies without repeatedly
deriving them from raw trajectories. However, errors in stored
abstractions can propagate to subsequent decisions through retrieval and
reuse. They can also shape execution trajectories, which then become the
basis for new abstractions that reproduce the original errors. We term
this feedback mechanism _error reproduction_: errors are regenerated
through a cycle of abstraction, execution, and re-abstraction, extending
their persistence beyond direct reuse of the original faulty knowledge.
We propose Anti-Persistence, a memory design that accumulates
trajectories and outcomes while reconstructing task-specific guidance on
demand. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to decide whether and
how to synthesize guidance, which is discarded after execution. This
prevents its direct reuse as a stored object, although indirect feedback
through retained trajectories remains possible. Across different
benchmarks and backbones, Anti-Persistence achieves higher overall
held-out success and the lowest average LLM-call cost among the
evaluated memory designs. These results support separating experience
accumulation from abstraction persistence in memory-based
self-improvement.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents solve tasks through multi-step
interactions with an environment, producing trajectories of actions and
observations \[[31](#bib.bib1)\]. We study _memory-based
self-improvement_, in which an agent stores experience and outcomes from
its own executions in external memory, retrieves that memory to guide
later tasks, and updates it with the resulting experience
\[[18](#bib.bib2), [35](#bib.bib3), [21](#bib.bib4), [23](#bib.bib5)\].
Together, repeated execution, memory updates, and reuse form a feedback
loop across tasks \[[27](#bib.bib6), [4](#bib.bib8)\]: with the LLM
parameters held fixed, the agent adapts through changes in the
experience available for decision-making and in how that experience is
used. Although this process is intended to improve subsequent
performance, its effectiveness must be established empirically, because
the content retained by the agent can affect both the next task and
later rounds of adaptation.

Stored experience can take the form of observed interaction records,
which preserve trajectories and task outcomes, or inferred abstractions,
which express rules, skills, summaries, or heuristics derived from those
records. Because long interaction histories contain both reusable
procedures and episode-specific details, distilling them into compact
guidance can make relevant experience easier to retrieve and use. Many
agent systems therefore extract abstractions from past executions and
retain them for subsequent tasks. This compression nevertheless requires
judgments about which details matter and under what conditions a pattern
generalizes; a rule that succeeds in one task may depend on conditions
absent from another. The value of abstraction thus depends not only on
identifying a useful pattern but also on reassessing its applicability
when it is reused.

The effects of a mistaken abstraction can extend beyond the task in
which it is retrieved and used. A stored rule can influence an agent’s
actions, and the resulting execution records may become inputs for
synthesizing new abstractions in subsequent self-improvement rounds
([Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
Even when the original rule is not supplied to the synthesis step, these
records may still contain erroneous actions taken under its guidance.
When extracting lessons from these records, the agent may infer a new
rule that reproduces the same error, allowing the error to persist
indirectly through execution history. We call this possible feedback
mechanism _error reproduction_, distinguishing the reappearance of an
error in a newly generated abstraction from its propagation through
retrieval and reuse. Both trajectories and abstractions can carry
influence across tasks, with the extent of that influence depending on
how the stored content is retrieved and used.

Memory maintenance can improve stored content through scoring, pruning,
or refinement \[[15](#bib.bib14)\], but deleting an abstraction does not
by itself revise trajectories generated under its influence or remove
abstractions subsequently derived from those trajectories. Whether
reproduction continues depends jointly on which records are retrieved,
what is synthesized from them, and which outputs are admitted to memory.
These dependencies motivate examining the need for inferred content to
persist alongside the procedures used to maintain it, leading to the
following question:

How can LLM agents benefit from abstraction in memory-based
self-improvement while limiting error reproduction?

We propose Anti-Persistence, a memory module that retains observed
interaction records while synthesizing abstractions for the current
task. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to determine whether and
how to transform retrieved experience into guidance, which supports the
current execution and is discarded afterward. Subsequent tasks can
revisit the accumulated records to construct guidance suited to their
own context, allowing the agent to adapt through experience accumulation
and mode selection while the synthesis procedure remains fixed and its
outputs remain temporary. Our contributions are threefold.

- •
  We introduce a memory design for self-improvement that separates the
  accumulation of execution experience from the temporary use of
  abstractions. Raw trajectories and task outcomes are retained, while
  inferred rules, summaries, and heuristics are used only for the
  current task and discarded afterward.
- •
  We develop an adaptive mode selector for on-demand abstraction that
  chooses between using retrieved records directly and synthesizing
  behavioral patterns, task strategies, or corrective guidance for each
  task. This enables a fixed synthesis procedure to support successive
  tasks without persisting its outputs.
- •
  We evaluate multiple rounds of self-improvement across three
  benchmarks and three backbones. Anti-Persistence achieves a higher
  overall success rate on held-out tasks at a lower average LLM-call
  cost. We also find associations between earlier and subsequently
  generated abstractions, providing empirical evidence consistent with
  error reproduction.

Figure 1: Error propagation and reproduction in agent memory. Left: An
illustrative error in a stored trajectory is reused through retrieval.
Center: A faulty inferred rule may shape later trajectories and be
encoded again through subsequent synthesis. Right: Possible routes of
influence. Both designs can retain feedback through stored trajectories;
the examples imply neither a fixed ordering of their reach nor
inevitable amplification.

## 2 Related Work

Memory-based self-improvement in LLM agents. External memory allows
agents to incorporate their own interaction experience into later
decisions \[[31](#bib.bib1), [21](#bib.bib4)\], with existing approaches
differing in the content retained across updates. Trajectory-based
methods store raw or lightly processed episodes for similarity-based
retrieval \[[27](#bib.bib6), [4](#bib.bib8)\], whereas other methods
retain verbal reflections, cross-task rules, summaries, or executable
skills \[[18](#bib.bib2), [35](#bib.bib3), [23](#bib.bib5),
[3](#bib.bib13), [29](#bib.bib12), [33](#bib.bib15)\]. Related forms of
abstraction also appear in production agent systems \[[32](#bib.bib9),
[28](#bib.bib10), [25](#bib.bib11)\]. We examine how the choice of
persistent content affects later memory updates through the trajectories
it helps generate.

Error propagation in iterative systems. Prior work examines how
generated content can bias later behavior through repeated use
\[[27](#bib.bib6), [26](#bib.bib19), [1](#bib.bib20)\], while related
model-collapse studies show that repeated training on self-generated
data can reduce distributional fidelity \[[20](#bib.bib7),
[17](#bib.bib21), [7](#bib.bib17), [6](#bib.bib18)\]. Although parameter
training differs from the external-memory updates studied here, these
findings motivate examining feedback from generated experience. We focus
on _error reproduction_, in which abstractions shape trajectories that
inform subsequent synthesis: propagation concerns how an existing error
affects behavior, whereas reproduction concerns whether that influence
is encoded in a new abstraction. Because deleting the original
abstraction does not by itself remove stored descendants, this
dependence on earlier outputs creates a possible feedback loop across
iterations \[[14](#bib.bib22), [12](#bib.bib23)\], even though
maintenance can also target the descendant entries.

Memory maintenance and reliability. Related approaches improve memory or
agent reliability through pruning, scoring, refinement, and learned
operations \[[15](#bib.bib14), [11](#bib.bib24), [13](#bib.bib25),
[9](#bib.bib26), [16](#bib.bib27), [36](#bib.bib28)\]. In systems that
retain abstractions, these maintenance procedures determine which
inferred content remains available for direct retrieval across tasks.
Anti-Persistence addresses the complementary question of persistence by
synthesizing task-specific abstractions on demand and discarding them
after use, while retaining the resulting trajectories for later
retrieval and synthesis. This design removes direct abstraction reuse
but still permits indirect feedback through experience.

## 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents

Anti-Persistence constructs temporary guidance from accumulated
interaction records, combining on-demand synthesis with adaptive mode
selection. We first formalize the memory update process and then
describe how these components support task execution.

### 3.1 Preliminaries

We consider an agent with fixed backbone parameters $`\theta`$ that
processes a sequence of tasks, receiving task $`\tau_{k}`$ and producing
trajectory $`e_{k}`$ and outcome $`y_{k}`$ at training-task update
$`k`$. Each experimental iteration $`\ell`$ comprises multiple such
updates followed by held-out evaluation with memory and related state
frozen.

Memory. The agent maintains a trajectory memory
$`M_{k}=\{(\tau_{j},e_{j},y_{j}):j<k\},`$ which stores previous
executions and their outcomes. An operator $`\phi`$ generates an
abstraction from the available records:
$`s=\phi(H),\quad H\subseteq M,`$ where $`M`$ is the trajectory store
available at synthesis time, with task, mode, and decoding arguments
omitted for clarity. The abstraction store $`S_{k}`$ contains the
summaries, rules, strategies, or skills currently retained; because
maintenance may delete or transform entries, it need not include every
abstraction generated previously.

Retrieval and generation. Given a new task $`\tau_{k}`$, the agent
retrieves a context $`C_{k}=R(\tau_{k},M_{k}\cup S_{k},B),`$ where $`R`$
is a retrieval operator and $`B`$ is the retrieval budget. The agent
then generates a trajectory according to
$`e_{k}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\tau_{k},C_{k}),`$ where
$`\pi_{\theta}`$ denotes the underlying policy, such as an LLM-based
agent.

Memory update. After each task, the agent stores the task, execution
trajectory, and outcome:
$`M_{k+1}=M_{k}\cup\{(\tau_{k},e_{k},y_{k})\}.`$ Methods that retain
abstractions also update a separate store $`S_{k}`$. Let
$`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ denote new candidates synthesized from available
records. Then
$`S_{k+1}=\mathcal{U}_{k}(S_{k},\mathcal{A}_{k};M_{k+1}).`$ Here,
$`\mathcal{U}_{k}`$ decides how to incorporate these candidates and
maintain existing entries, with $`M_{k+1}`$ available as evidence. It
may simply append all candidates or apply filtering, pruning, or
merging.

Anti-persistence updates $`M_{k}`$ but keeps $`S_{k}=\emptyset`$:
guidance generated for the current task is discarded after execution.
The execution records remain available for later retrieval and
synthesis.

Feedback through experience. A stored abstraction
$`s_{\mathrm{parent}}`$ can enter the agent’s context during task
execution, which produces trajectory $`e_{j}`$. Once execution is
complete, its record may be included in retrieved records $`H`$ and used
to synthesize a new abstraction $`s_{\mathrm{candidate}}`$:
$`s_{\mathrm{parent}}\longrightarrow e_{j}\longrightarrow H\longrightarrow s_{\mathrm{candidate}}.`$
An error in the old abstraction may thus influence execution and
reappear in newly synthesized guidance. Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Reproduction Dynamics in Abstraction Memory ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
separately analyzes exposure to flagged abstractions, generation of
flagged candidates, and their admission to persistent memory.

Algorithm 1 Anti-Persistence: local mode selection and task execution

### 3.2 Algorithm Design

Anti-persistence separates the use of an abstraction from its storage
for later reuse
([Section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Preliminaries ‣ 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
It retrieves interaction records, generates guidance when needed, and
discards that guidance after execution.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

What persists. The agent retains two kinds of records. Trajectory memory
$`M_{k}`$ stores tasks, executions, and outcomes that can be retrieved
as examples. The outcome log $`\mathcal{L}_{k}`$, defined below, records
mode choices and their feedback to support later choices. Neither store
retains synthesized guidance, and the abstraction store $`S_{k}`$
remains empty.

These records preserve what occurred, without certifying that the
agent’s actions or explanations were correct. Temporary guidance may
affect a stored trajectory and thereby influence later synthesis.
Discarding guidance therefore prevents its direct reuse as a stored
object but leaves indirect feedback through trajectories possible.

How to use retrieved experience. For each task, the agent chooses
whether to use interaction records directly or synthesize guidance from
them. We define four modes:

|     |                                                                                                                 |     |     |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}=\{\mathrm{none},\;\mathrm{imitation},\;\mathrm{strategic},\;\mathrm{corrective}\}.`$ |     | (1) |

The $`\mathrm{none}`$ mode supplies retrieved records directly, so it
uses memory without an additional synthesis call. The
$`\mathrm{imitation}`$ mode extracts reusable action patterns and their
conditions from successful trajectories. The $`\mathrm{strategic}`$ mode
uses successful trajectories to organize higher-level subgoals and
plans. The $`\mathrm{corrective}`$ mode analyzes failed trajectories to
generate avoidance guidance, using a successful trajectory as a contrast
when available. Full definitions appear in
[Section B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Abstraction Modes ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").

Feedback for mode selection. The agent uses past outcomes to assess
which mode may suit the current task. We formulate this choice as a
lightweight contextual bandit over $`\mathcal{Z}`$, supported by the
outcome log

|     |                                                                                                      |     |     |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{k}=\{(\tau_{j},\mu_{j},y_{j},r_{j},t_{j}):j<k,\ j\in\mathcal{J}_{k}\},`$ |     | (2) |

where $`\mathcal{J}_{k}`$ indexes eligible completed attempts
([Section B.5](#A2.SS5 "B.5 Outcome-Log Schema and Update Protocol ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
Each entry records the task, selected mode, raw outcome $`y_{j}`$,
cost-adjusted reward $`r_{j}`$, and logical timestamp $`t_{j}`$. The
reward guides mode selection, while the raw outcome preserves task
performance separately from the cost penalty.

Two retrieval steps. On the local-selection branch, the controller first
retrieves similar tasks from $`\mathcal{L}_{k}`$ to choose a mode. It
then retrieves trajectories from $`M_{k}`$ according to that mode. The
first retrieval supplies feedback for choosing how to use experience;
the second supplies the experience itself. Their budgets are $`\hat{B}`$
and the mode-specific base budget $`B`$, respectively.

Selecting a mode from local feedback. For task $`\tau`$, the first
retrieval returns up to $`\hat{B}`$ nearest outcome-log entries,
$`\mathcal{N}_{\hat{B}}(\tau)=\{(\tau_{i},\mu_{i},y_{i},r_{i},t_{i})\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\hat{B}}(\tau)}.`$
The controller compares modes using their recorded rewards, weighted by
relevance and recency.

Cost-adjusted reward. Each attempt receives a reward that combines task
outcome with additional synthesis cost,
$`r_{i}=\operatorname{clip}(y_{i}-\lambda\kappa_{i},-1,1),`$ where
$`\kappa_{i}`$ counts actual extra synthesis calls, including zero when
synthesis is skipped. The coefficient $`\lambda\geq 0`$ controls the
penalty, which applies only to synthesis calls.

Relevance weighting. Each retrieved entry receives a weight based on
task similarity and recency,
$`w_{i}=\max(\mathrm{sim}(\tau_{i},\tau),0)\cdot\gamma^{t_{\max}-t_{i}},`$
where $`t_{\max}`$ is the latest timestamp in the retrieved neighborhood
and $`\gamma\in(0,1]`$ controls the weight of older feedback. Anchoring
at $`t_{\max}`$ rescales all $`\gamma^{k-t_{i}}`$ weights equally and
leaves normalized estimates unchanged. Decay affects only mode-selection
feedback, without changing trajectory retrieval. An older mode
evaluation may become less representative as memory grows, even when its
trajectory remains a useful example.

Local utility estimation. For each mode, the controller averages the
rewards of retrieved attempts that used it. If their total weight is
positive, $`\sum_{i:\mu_{i}=\mu}w_{i}>0`$, the estimate is

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\hat{r}(\mu\mid\tau)=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\hat{B}}(\tau):\,\mu_{i}=\mu}w_{i}r_{i}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\hat{B}}(\tau):\,\mu_{i}=\mu}w_{i}}.
``` |  |

This estimate summarizes the mode’s observed performance and synthesis
cost on similar tasks.

Mode selection. The controller adds an exploration bonus to this
estimate and selects the highest-scoring mode:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mu^{\star}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\arg\max_{\mu\in\mathcal{Z}}\Bigg(\hat{r}(\mu\mid\tau)+c\sqrt{\frac{\log|\mathcal{N}_{\hat{B}}(\tau)|}{\max(n_{\mu},1)}}\Bigg),`$ |  | (3) |

where
$`n_{\mu}=\left|\{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\hat{B}}(\tau):\mu_{i}=\mu\}\right|.`$
Here, $`n_{\mu}`$ counts retrieved attempts using mode $`\mu`$. For
$`c>0`$, the bonus encourages revisiting modes with fewer local
observations. This UCB-inspired rule balances observed reward with
exploration. It carries no confidence-bound or regret guarantee for
weighted, nonstationary observations. Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.1 Preliminaries ‣ 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
describes the local branch with a nonempty trusted neighborhood and
positive weight for every compared mode. Unsupported means are
undefined; initialization, fallback, and exploration overrides use
separate branches
([Section B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).

Execution and feedback. After selection, the agent retrieves
mode-appropriate trajectories, uses them directly or synthesizes
temporary guidance, and executes the task. During training, execution
records enter $`M_{k}`$ and eligible feedback enters
$`\mathcal{L}_{k}`$. Guidance is discarded after use; evaluation leaves
both stores unchanged. New records change subsequent estimates and
choices. The backbone, mode definitions, synthesis prompts, retrieval
procedures, and selection rule remain fixed.

## 4 Experiments

We evaluate held-out success and cost
([Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Held-Out Performance and LLM-Call Cost ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
performance across memory updates
([Section 4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Dynamics Across Self-Improvement Rounds ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
and individual design choices
([Section 4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Ablations and Design Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
Provenance associations
([Section E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Provenance Associations and Operational Bias Flags ‣ Appendix E Extended Cross-Backbone Results ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents"))
and controlled content and retention studies
([Appendix F](#A6 "Appendix F Additional Controlled and Statistical Analyses ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents"))
provide complementary evidence about the role of inferred guidance.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks. We evaluate anti-persistence on ALFWorld
\[[19](#bib.bib33)\], WebShop \[[30](#bib.bib34)\], and ScienceWorld
\[[24](#bib.bib35)\], using fixed training and held-out task partitions
across methods and iterations following recent agent-memory work
\[[35](#bib.bib3), [3](#bib.bib13), [18](#bib.bib2), [4](#bib.bib8)\].
Partition sizes are reported in
[Table 4](#A4.T4 "In D.1 Per-Benchmark Task Counts and Partitioning ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").

Backbones. The main experiments use Llama-4-Scout \[[10](#bib.bib29)\],
Qwen3-Coder-Next \[[2](#bib.bib30)\], and Gemma-4-31B-it
\[[8](#bib.bib32)\], spanning distinct model families and capabilities
to examine how memory effects vary across backbones.

Baselines. We compare four memory configurations: trajectory memory
retrieves stored trajectories, abstraction memory retrieves stored
inferred abstractions, joint memory retrieves both, and anti-persistence
constructs temporary guidance from stored trajectories. We also evaluate
four agent baselines: ReAct \[[31](#bib.bib1)\], Reflexion
\[[18](#bib.bib2)\], ExpeL \[[35](#bib.bib3)\], and AutoRefine
\[[15](#bib.bib14)\].

Protocol. Each method undergoes $`K=10`$ iterations with fixed backbone
parameters, with memory and related state updated exclusively from
training episodes. After each iteration, we evaluate the full held-out
set with this state frozen: retrieval is permitted, but stored
trajectories, abstractions, outcome logs, retrieval metadata,
maintenance scores, and pruning decisions remain unchanged, and
evaluation logs never enter subsequent updates. Under a shared per-task
context budget, the base trajectory-retrieval budget is $`B=5`$, with
one additional successful trajectory available as a contrast for
corrective mode
([Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Retrieval Similarity ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
Anti-persistence uses up to $`\hat{B}=10`$ outcome-log entries for mode
selection.

Metrics. We report held-out success over 3 seeds ({42,43,44}), with
error bars denoting standard deviations across seeds, and measure cost
as the mean number of synthesis and execution LLM calls per held-out
task.

### 4.2 Held-Out Performance and LLM-Call Cost

[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.2 Algorithm Design ‣ 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
compares held-out success at $`K=10`$ against four agent baselines and
three persistent-memory variants.
[Figure 3](#S4.F3 "In 4.2 Held-Out Performance and LLM-Call Cost ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
reports average per-task LLM-call cost for the four memory
configurations.

(a) Per-iteration held-out task success rate.

(b) Per-iteration mean trajectory length.

Figure 2: Per-iteration performance of four memory configurations over
ten memory-update iterations across three benchmarks and two backbones.

Anti-persistence improves overall held-out success. Anti-persistence
achieved the highest success rate in seven of the nine
benchmark–backbone settings
([Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.2 Algorithm Design ‣ 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
Averaged equally across settings, it reached $`59.9\%`$, compared with
$`53.5\%`$ for trajectory memory, $`49.0\%`$ for abstraction memory, and
$`49.3\%`$ for joint memory. It achieved higher mean success than
trajectory and abstraction memory in all nine settings, and joint memory
in eight. It also exceeded Reflexion, the strongest agent baseline on
average, which reached $`52.9\%`$. The memory variants further clarify
the role of stored abstractions: both abstraction memory and joint
memory underperformed trajectory memory in seven of the nine settings.
Retaining inferred guidance, either alone or alongside execution
records, therefore did not consistently improve success. These
comparisons favor anti-persistence overall while leaving the preferred
design setting-dependent. Section
[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Dynamics Across Self-Improvement Rounds ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
examines how these differences develop across updates.

Figure 3: Mean LLM-call cost and held-out success across nine settings.

Anti-persistence has the lowest average LLM-call cost. Across the nine
settings, anti-persistence achieved the lowest mean LLM-call cost among
the four memory configurations, alongside the highest mean success
([Figure 3](#S4.F3 "In 4.2 Held-Out Performance and LLM-Call Cost ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
Generating temporary guidance therefore did not translate into a higher
average call count. Total call usage reflects both guidance synthesis
and task execution. The $`\mathrm{none}`$ mode reuses retrieved
trajectories directly without a synthesis call, while shorter execution
trajectories in some settings offset calls used to construct guidance.
These results support the efficiency of direct experience reuse and
selective synthesis.

### 4.3 Dynamics Across Self-Improvement Rounds

To characterize behavior across memory updates, we first examine how the
four memory configurations perform over successive rounds
([Figure 2](#S4.F2 "In 4.2 Held-Out Performance and LLM-Call Cost ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
We then compare the final results of abstraction memory, AutoRefine, and
anti-persistence
([Figure 7](#S4.F7 "In 4.3 Dynamics Across Self-Improvement Rounds ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).

Memory Behavior Across Iterations. Memory effects varied across
backbones and benchmarks
([Figure 2](#S4.F2 "In 4.2 Held-Out Performance and LLM-Call Cost ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
Anti-persistence achieved the highest final mean success in all six
settings, although it did not lead at every iteration. Qwen’s
abstraction-memory performance fluctuated more on WebShop than on
ALFWorld, while Llama’s joint-memory performance declined in later
rounds, particularly on ScienceWorld. These trajectories show that
combining trajectory and abstraction memory did not consistently improve
performance. Trajectory length provides complementary context
([Figure 2(b)](#S4.F2.sf2 "In Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Held-Out Performance and LLM-Call Cost ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
but shorter rollouts can reflect either efficient execution or early
failure. Their coincidence with lower success under joint memory is
consistent with premature termination, without establishing its cause.

Comparison with Memory Maintenance.
[Figure 7](#S4.F7 "In 4.3 Dynamics Across Self-Improvement Rounds ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
presents the final results for abstraction memory, AutoRefine, and
anti-persistence from
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.2 Algorithm Design ‣ 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").
AutoRefine improved mean success over abstraction memory in one of the
six settings, matched it in one, and performed worse in four.
Anti-persistence achieved higher mean success than AutoRefine in all
six. AutoRefine also changes retrieval and synthesis
([Section D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 AutoRefine Baseline Implementation ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
so this comparison does not isolate maintenance effects or rule out more
effective policies. Deleting an abstraction leaves stored trajectories
unchanged unless they are explicitly revised (Remark
[1](#Thmremark1 "Remark 1 (Scope of parent deletion). ‣ A.3 What Deletion and Maintenance Do Establish ‣ Appendix A Reproduction Dynamics in Abstraction Memory ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
Maintenance can nevertheless affect subsequent exposure, flagged
generation, and persistent admission (Proposition
[1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (One-step generation and retention of flagged abstractions). ‣ A.3 What Deletion and Maintenance Do Establish ‣ Appendix A Reproduction Dynamics in Abstraction Memory ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).

Figure 4: Final held-out success for abstraction memory, AutoRefine, and
anti-persistence from
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.2 Algorithm Design ‣ 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").
Bars show means over 3 seeds; error bars show standard deviations.

Figure 5: Sensitivity to recency decay $`\gamma`$ on Qwen3-Coder-Next.
Bars show means over $`3`$ seeds; error bars show standard deviation
across seeds.

Figure 6: Mode-selection ablation on Qwen3-Coder-Next, comparing
anti-persistence’s contextual bandit with fixed-mode and random
policies.

Figure 7: Sensitivity to $`\lambda`$ on Qwen3-Coder-Next. Solid curves
use the left axis for success rate; dashed curves use the right axis for
synthesis-mode usage (fraction of tasks selecting a synthesis mode).

### 4.4 Ablations and Design Analysis

Sensitivity to Recency Decay $`\gamma`$. The recency factor $`\gamma`$
controls how quickly older outcome-log feedback loses weight during mode
selection. Smaller values discount older feedback more strongly, whereas
$`\gamma=1`$ removes temporal decay while retaining task-similarity
weighting.
[Figure 7](#S4.F7 "In 4.3 Dynamics Across Self-Improvement Rounds ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
compares four values on Qwen3-Coder-Next. The default $`\gamma=0.998`$
achieved the highest mean success among the tested values: $`96.0\%`$ on
ALFWorld and $`54.0\%`$ on WebShop. At $`\gamma=0.980`$, success was
$`90.0\%`$ on ALFWorld and $`48.7\%`$ on WebShop; at $`\gamma=0.990`$,
it was $`87.3\%`$ and $`44.7\%`$, respectively. Without decay
($`\gamma=1`$), success was $`88.7\%`$ and $`48.7\%`$. Both faster decay
and no decay therefore underperformed the default. These results favor
retaining historical feedback while modestly emphasizing recent
outcomes, although success did not vary monotonically with $`\gamma`$.

Benefits of Adaptive Mode Selection. To assess the value of adapting
mode selection to tasks and feedback,
[Figure 7](#S4.F7 "In 4.3 Dynamics Across Self-Improvement Rounds ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
compares the contextual bandit with fixed strategic, imitation, and
corrective policies and with random selection on Qwen3-Coder-Next. The
bandit achieved the highest success rate on both ALFWorld ($`96.0\%`$)
and WebShop ($`54.0\%`$). The strongest fixed policy differed by
benchmark: strategic performed best on ALFWorld and imitation on
WebShop. The bandit’s advantage over fixed and random selection supports
using task context and accumulated feedback to decide how retrieved
experience should guide execution.

Sensitivity to Cost Weight $`\lambda`$. The cost weight $`\lambda`$
penalizes additional synthesis calls in the mode-selection reward;
$`\lambda=0`$ removes this penalty.
[Figure 7](#S4.F7 "In 4.3 Dynamics Across Self-Improvement Rounds ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
compares success and synthesis-mode usage across cost weights. The
default $`\lambda=0.05`$ achieved the highest mean success among the
tested values on both ALFWorld ($`96.0\%`$) and WebShop ($`54.0\%`$),
consistent with
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.2 Algorithm Design ‣ 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").
Removing the penalty increased synthesis-mode usage but reduced mean
success relative to the default; stronger penalties
($`\lambda\in\{0.20,0.50\}`$) reduced both. These results favor
selective synthesis with a modest penalty in the tested settings. Usage
is the fraction of tasks selecting a synthesis mode, even when missing
records prevent an actual call.

Mode Selection Patterns Across Settings. To examine how the controller
allocated modes across settings,
[Figure 8](#S4.F8 "In 4.4 Ablations and Design Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
reports selection frequencies averaged over iterations for nine
$`(\text{backbone}\times\text{benchmark})`$ combinations. All settings
used multiple modes. On WebShop, stronger backbones favored
$`\mathrm{imitation}`$ and Llama-4-Scout favored $`\mathrm{strategic}`$,
while ALFWorld and ScienceWorld showed more balanced usage. The
$`\mathrm{none}`$ mode, which reuses retrieved trajectories without
synthesis, had a nonzero mean frequency in every setting, so the
controller sometimes reused experience directly. These averages describe
overall allocation, without showing whether a mode was selected in every
round or establishing policy convergence.

| Model            | Bench | Discard (Ours) | Persist        | $`\Delta`$ |
|------------------|-------|----------------|----------------|------------|
| Llama-4-Scout    | ALF   | 54.7$`\pm`$2.9 | 26.7$`\pm`$6.1 | +28.0      |
| Llama-4-Scout    | Web   | 46.3$`\pm`$1.8 | 34.0$`\pm`$4.0 | +12.3      |
| Qwen3-Coder-Next | ALF   | 96.0$`\pm`$1.4 | 92.7$`\pm`$1.2 | 0+3.3      |
| Qwen3-Coder-Next | Web   | 54.0$`\pm`$2.0 | 47.3$`\pm`$3.1 | 0+6.7      |

Table 2: Held-out success with abstractions persisted or discarded (%,
mean $`\pm`$ s.d.; 3 seeds).

Persisting versus Discarding Abstractions. To assess abstraction
persistence, we compared variants that used synthesized guidance for the
current task when synthesis was invoked, but differed in whether it was
subsequently discarded or stored for later retrieval. Discarding
improved success in all four settings
([Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.4 Ablations and Design Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
with larger gains for Llama-4-Scout and positive gains for
Qwen3-Coder-Next. These comparisons favor using synthesized guidance
temporarily, without storing it for later tasks, in the evaluated
settings.

Figure 8: Mode-selection frequencies averaged over iterations
$`1`$–$`10`$. Panels denote benchmarks, rows denote backbones, and
columns denote modes ($`\mathrm{none}`$, imitation, strategic,
corrective). Darker cells indicate more frequent selection.

## 5 Conclusion

We introduced anti-persistence for memory-based self-improvement: agents
accumulate trajectories and outcomes and adaptively construct temporary
guidance with a fixed backbone and synthesis procedure. The design
removes direct storage and reuse of synthesized abstractions, while
indirect feedback through trajectories remains possible. Our analysis
distinguishes exposure, flagged generation, and persistent admission
without implying that all maintenance policies fail. Across three
benchmarks and three backbones, anti-persistence achieved higher overall
held-out success with fewer LLM calls on average. These findings support
separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence and
studying when verification can justify selective retention.

## Contents of the Appendix

## Appendix A Reproduction Dynamics in Abstraction Memory

This appendix formalizes the relationship between historical exposure to
stored abstractions and the generation and retention of flagged
candidates by distinguishing provenance, operational bias labels, and
admission to persistent memory. Each abstraction symbol denotes a
unique, immutable object identifier to which labels and parent sets
refer; rewriting or merging creates a new identifier. The results
concern a single synthesis invocation under stated conditions and
establish neither progressive improvement nor inevitable long-run
degradation, nor do they imply that all maintenance policies fail.

### A.1 Operational Bias Labels and Historical Provenance

###### Definition 1 (Operational bias labels).

Fix an evaluation and labeling protocol $`\mathcal{E}`$. Let
$`\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{lab}}`$ be the abstractions with defined labels
under that protocol, and let
$`b_{\mathcal{E}}:\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{lab}}\to\{0,1\}`$. Define the
flagged set

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{E}}=\{s\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{lab}}:b_{\mathcal{E}}(s)=1\}.
``` |  |

An abstraction in $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{E}}`$ is called operationally
biased. Abstractions outside $`\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{lab}}`$ are
unclassified; absence of a flag does not certify that an abstraction is
benign.

The evaluation protocol and resulting labels remain fixed within each
theoretical comparison, so all probability statements below concern
operational flags rather than an unobserved intrinsic error rate. Our
empirical protocol assigns these labels using associations with
downstream success
([Section E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Provenance Associations and Operational Bias Flags ‣ Appendix E Extended Cross-Backbone Results ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
which do not identify the causal effect of an abstraction.

#### Historical provenance.

For a stored execution record $`m_{j}=(\tau_{j},e_{j},y_{j})`$, let
$`P(m_{j})`$ contain the identifiers of persistent abstractions
retrieved into the agent’s context when $`e_{j}`$ was generated. These
identifiers remain attached to the record for analysis even after the
corresponding abstractions are deleted, documenting historical exposure
without by themselves establishing behavioral influence.

For a synthesis input $`H\subseteq M_{k}`$, define its historical parent
set and flagged-parent exposure event by

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P(H)=\bigcup_{m\in H}P(m),\qquad C=\{P(H)\cap\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{E}}\neq\emptyset\}.
``` |  |

Execution records and abstraction identifiers remain distinct types
throughout this analysis, and every parent in $`P(m_{j})`$ must have
existed when the record was generated, so parent sets never depend on
future trajectories. We call $`C`$ an “exposed input” event without
assuming that the input inherited any particular error from a parent.

For each synthesized candidate $`s=\phi(H)`$, record $`P(s)=P(H)`$ at
creation. A directed edge $`u\to s`$ exists when $`u\in P(s)`$;
descendants are objects reachable along these recorded synthesis edges,
excluding the starting object itself.

### A.2 Exposure, Generation, and Persistent Admission

Consider a single synthesis invocation conditional on a fixed
post-maintenance state, with its probability law encompassing task and
mode selection, input retrieval, and synthesis randomness. Writing the
candidate output as $`s=\phi(H)`$ with other conditioning arguments
suppressed, define

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A=\{s\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{E}}\},\qquad W=\{s\text{ is admitted as the same object to persistent abstraction memory}\}.
``` |  |

Rewriting or merging a candidate creates a new object requiring its own
label and admission analysis; all probabilities below refer to the same
fixed state and probability law for the invocation.

###### Definition 2 (Conditional reproduction coefficient).

Let $`q=\Pr(C)`$. If $`q>0`$, define

|     |                      |     |
|-----|----------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \alpha=\Pr(A\mid C).
       ```                   |     |

If $`\Pr(A\cap C)>0`$, also define the conditional admission probability

|     |                          |     |
|-----|--------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \eta=\Pr(W\mid A\cap C).
       ```                       |     |

The coefficient $`\alpha`$ is the flagged-output rate conditional on
flagged-parent exposure. It is not an offspring count, a causal effect,
or a growth factor.

These quantities may vary with the state, retrieval policy, synthesis
operator, and maintenance procedure. A positive $`\alpha`$ alone
establishes neither an increase in the flagged-output rate relative to
other inputs nor the accumulation of errors across successive
iterations.

### A.3 What Deletion and Maintenance Do Establish

###### Remark 1 (Scope of parent deletion).

Immediately before a deletion-only operation, let $`S^{-}`$ be the
abstraction store and $`D^{-}\subseteq S^{-}`$ its currently retained
descendants of a parent $`s_{0}`$. Descendants are identified by the
historical provenance relation above, possibly over multiple
generations, and exclude $`s_{0}`$ itself. If the operation deletes
$`R\subseteq S^{-}`$ and does not alter execution records or their
provenance, then

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
S^{+}=S^{-}\setminus R,\qquad D^{+}=D^{-}\setminus R,\qquad M^{+}=M^{-}.
``` |  |

In particular, deleting only $`s_{0}`$ leaves $`D^{-}`$ unchanged,
whereas deleting descendants can remove them. Removing a parent does not
automatically erase its recorded history, but the remaining influence
need not be irreversible.

These identities follow directly from the specified deletion operation,
without implying that descendants survive other maintenance steps or
that retained records are necessarily retrieved again.

###### Proposition 1 (One-step generation and retention of flagged abstractions).

Under the common law specified above, suppose $`q>0`$. Then

|     |                                                |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Pr(A\cap C)=q\alpha,\qquad\Pr(A)\geq q\alpha.
       ```                                             |     |

If $`q\alpha>0`$, then

|     |                                                                    |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Pr(A\cap C\cap W)=q\alpha\eta,\qquad\Pr(A\cap W)\geq q\alpha\eta.
       ```                                                                 |     |

Thus, positive $`q`$, $`\alpha`$, and $`\eta`$ imply a positive
probability of generating and admitting a flagged candidate with
flagged-parent exposure.

###### Proof.

Since $`q>0`$, the definition of conditional probability gives
$`\Pr(A\cap C)=\Pr(C)\Pr(A\mid C)=q\alpha`$. The inclusion
$`A\cap C\subseteq A`$ gives the first inequality. If $`q\alpha>0`$,
conditioning on $`A\cap C`$ yields
$`\Pr(A\cap C\cap W)=\Pr(A\cap C)\Pr(W\mid A\cap C)=q\alpha\eta`$. The
inclusion $`A\cap C\cap W\subseteq A\cap W`$ gives the second
inequality. No independence assumption is required. ∎

When $`q=0`$, flagged-parent exposure has zero probability and
$`\alpha`$ is undefined; when $`q>0`$ but $`\alpha=0`$, generating a
flagged candidate with flagged-parent exposure has zero probability and
$`\eta`$ is undefined. Neither case justifies assigning a value to the
undefined conditional quantity.

#### Scope of the result.

Proposition
[1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (One-step generation and retention of flagged abstractions). ‣ A.3 What Deletion and Maintenance Do Establish ‣ Appendix A Reproduction Dynamics in Abstraction Memory ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
provides a probability decomposition rather than a positive lower bound
valid across all maintenance policies, because maintenance may change
future exposure $`q`$, the conditional input or synthesis distribution
determining $`\alpha`$, and the admission probability $`\eta`$. For
example, excluding all exposed records sets $`q=0`$, while rejecting
every flagged candidate prevents flagged candidates from entering
persistent memory. By separating historical exposure, flagged
generation, and persistent admission within a single synthesis
invocation, the proposition identifies distinct components of the
process without establishing inevitable amplification or a long-horizon
performance ordering.

### A.4 Implications for Anti-Persistence

Because anti-persistence admits no synthesized candidate to the
abstraction store, $`W`$ is impossible and $`\Pr(A\cap W)=0`$ for every
task-time synthesis invocation. This storage property does not establish
$`\Pr(A)=0`$, since temporary abstractions may still be flagged and can
influence stored trajectories, subsequent synthesis, and mode selection.

The historical exposure event $`C`$ tracks previously stored
abstractions and therefore excludes feedback arising from temporary
guidance. In a fresh anti-persistence run with no stored ancestors,
$`q=0`$ and the corresponding $`\alpha`$ is undefined, not zero. Both
raw trajectories and abstractions can carry the effects of past
decisions into later tasks, with the extent of this influence determined
by retrieval and use rather than memory type alone. The structural
guarantee is consequently limited to the absence of stored abstractions
and their direct reuse, while the performance benefit remains an
empirical finding.

## Appendix B Method Details

This appendix specifies the abstraction modes, prompts, retrieval
procedures, and hyperparameters used by anti-persistence, together with
the outcome log that connects observed task results to subsequent mode
selection.

### B.1 Abstraction Modes

The mode set
$`\mathcal{Z}=\{\mathrm{none},\mathrm{imitation},\mathrm{strategic},\mathrm{corrective}\}`$
provides direct access to factual context or one of three forms of
on-demand abstraction, as introduced in
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").
While $`\mathrm{none}`$ passes retrieved records directly to the agent,
$`\mathrm{imitation}`$ extracts reusable behavioral patterns,
$`\mathrm{strategic}`$ develops higher-level task strategies, and
$`\mathrm{corrective}`$ generates guidance for avoiding observed
failures. When the required records are available, the three synthesis
modes invoke $`\phi`$ at task time and discard its output after
execution, using the input and output conventions in
[Section B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Mode-Specific Prompts ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").

#### $`\mu=\mathrm{none}`$ (direct factual context).

The agent receives factual context $`H_{\tau}`$, comprising retrieved
trajectory records and observed outcomes, directly without a synthesis
call, so $`\sigma_{\tau}=\phi(H_{\tau},\mathrm{none})=H_{\tau}`$ and
$`\kappa(\mathrm{none})=0`$. When no records are available, including at
initialization or after an embedding failure, $`H_{\tau}=\emptyset`$ and
the mode reduces to the underlying ReAct policy.

#### $`\mu=\mathrm{imitation}`$ (behavioral-pattern abstraction).

$`\phi`$ extracts reusable behavioral patterns from successful
trajectories, including action–observation sequences, tool-use routines,
and their applicability conditions, to provide task-specific guidance
without copying a trajectory verbatim. This mode emphasizes reusable
action patterns, whereas $`\mathrm{strategic}`$ focuses on higher-level
sub-goal organization and planning. The resulting abstraction is
injected under \## Behavioral Patterns (imitation) and discarded after
execution, with $`\kappa(\mathrm{imitation})=1`$ when synthesis is
invoked; if no successful trajectory is available,
$`\sigma_{\tau}=\emptyset`$ and no synthesis call is charged.

#### $`\mu=\mathrm{strategic}`$ (multi-trace strategy distillation).

$`\phi`$ uses up to the top-$`B`$ retrieved successful trajectories to
generate a strategy covering sub-goal structure, tool-use patterns, and
recovery heuristics, with a prompt that distinguishes transferable
structure from instance-specific details. The resulting guidance is
injected under \## Task-Specific Strategy (strategic reflection),
incurring $`\kappa(\mathrm{strategic})=1`$ when synthesis is invoked. If
no successful trajectories are available, $`\sigma_{\tau}=\emptyset`$
and no call is charged.

#### $`\mu=\mathrm{corrective}`$ (failure-driven avoidance rules).

$`\phi`$ uses up to the top-$`B`$ retrieved failure trajectories and one
contrasting success when available, prompting an LLM to identify failure
modes, critical decision points, and recurring error patterns. The
output consists of avoidance rules of the form “do NOT do $`X`$ because
$`Y`$,” optionally paired with corrective actions, and is injected under
\## Avoidance Rules (corrective reflection). Invoking synthesis incurs
$`\kappa(\mathrm{corrective})=1`$.

Design choice. When no failure trajectories are available, $`\phi`$
returns $`\sigma_{\tau}=\emptyset`$ rather than falling back to
$`\mathrm{strategic}`$, preventing strategic guidance from being
attributed to the $`\mathrm{corrective}`$ arm during bandit updates.

#### Cost convention.

We define $`\kappa(\mu)\geq 0`$ as the number of additional LLM calls
made by mode $`\mu`$ relative to direct trajectory reuse, so direct
factual context has $`\kappa(\mathrm{none})=0`$. Each synthesis mode
($`\mathrm{imitation}`$, $`\mathrm{strategic}`$, or
$`\mathrm{corrective}`$) incurs $`\kappa(\mu)=1`$ when invoked and zero
when synthesis is skipped because the required records are unavailable.
The cost weight $`\lambda`$ places these call counts on the reward scale
used for success outcomes, with defaults reported in
[Section B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").

### B.2 Mode-Specific Prompts

Each synthesis mode in
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
uses a prompt to produce $`\sigma_{\tau}`$ and a wrapper to present the
guidance under a mode-specific header in the agent’s context. We provide
the strategic and corrective templates, describe the imitation
interface, and specify the wrappers below, including the direct
factual-context wrapper used by $`\mathrm{none}`$ to bypass synthesis.

#### Strategic synthesis prompt.

The $`\mathrm{strategic}`$ mode prompts the synthesis LLM to distill a
transferable strategy from up to the top-$`B`$ retrieved successful
trajectories ($`B=5`$ by default).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The placeholders {instruction} and {success_text} contain the current
task description and up to the top-$`B`$ retrieved successful
trajectories, respectively, with trajectories concatenated as
$`\texttt{--- Success }i\texttt{ ---}`$ blocks. The synthesis LLM uses
temperature $`0`$ and a $`1024`$-token budget.

#### Corrective synthesis prompt.

The $`\mathrm{corrective}`$ mode prompts the synthesis LLM to extract
avoidance rules from up to the top-$`B`$ retrieved failure trajectories,
using a single successful trajectory as a contrast when available.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The placeholders {instruction} and {failure_text} contain the current
task description and up to the top-$`B`$ retrieved failures,
respectively. The placeholder {success_text} contains the top-1
successful trajectory when available and otherwise takes the value (no
successful reference available), allowing synthesis to proceed without a
positive reference. Decoding settings match those of the strategic
prompt.

#### Imitation synthesis interface.

Given the current task and up to the top-$`B`$ retrieved successful
trajectories, $`\mathrm{imitation}`$ identifies successful action
patterns, their supporting observations, and ways to adapt them to the
current task without generalizing instance-specific object names or
locations into rules. The synthesized guidance is presented through the
abstraction wrapper below rather than as a verbatim copy of a reference
trajectory.

#### Direct factual-context wrapper ($`\mathrm{none}`$).

The $`\mathrm{none}`$ mode supplies retrieved records and their observed
outcomes without a synthesis call, using the following factual-context
header:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Factual records retain their task instructions, observed outcomes, and
action–observation sequences within the shared context budget, with
formatting that adds no inferred behavioral rules and requires no
synthesis LLM call.

#### Injection wrapper.

The output of $`\mathrm{imitation}`$, $`\mathrm{strategic}`$, or
$`\mathrm{corrective}`$ receives a mode-specific markdown header before
being appended to the agent’s system prompt.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The headers Behavioral Patterns (imitation), Task-Specific Strategy
(strategic reflection), and Avoidance Rules (corrective reflection)
identify the source mode alongside each synthesized abstraction. Under
$`\mathrm{none}`$, the agent receives the factual-context wrapper above,
which is omitted only when no records are available.

### B.3 Retrieval Similarity

Both retrieval pathways operate on a fixed task embedding
$`\mathbf{e}_{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$ using the cosine similarity
function

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{sim}(\tau_{i},\tau)=\frac{\langle\mathbf{e}_{\tau_{i}},\mathbf{e}_{\tau}\rangle}{\lVert\mathbf{e}_{\tau_{i}}\rVert\cdot\lVert\mathbf{e}_{\tau}\rVert+\epsilon},\quad\epsilon=10^{-12},
``` |  |

but serve distinct purposes: *trajectory retrieval* selects records for
direct use or synthesis, whereas *mode-selection retrieval* selects
outcome-log neighbors for estimating local bandit rewards. These
purposes lead to differences in candidate sets, time decay, and
task-type filtering.

#### Task embedding.

For each task $`\tau`$, we compute one embedding by concatenating the
task instruction with a truncated prefix of the initial observation:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\texttt{embed\_text}=\texttt{instruction}\;\|\;\texttt{"Initial state:"}\;\|\;\texttt{truncate}(\texttt{obs},500).
``` |  |

Including the initial observation helps distinguish tasks that share a
goal template but differ in their starting state. Qwen3-Embedding-8B
\[[34](#bib.bib31)\] computes this embedding in a single API call; if
the call fails, $`\mathbf{e}_{\tau}`$ remains unset and the controller
defaults to $`\mu=\mathrm{none}`$ for the current task without an
in-iteration retry.

#### Trajectory retrieval (input to $`\phi`$).

Let $`R_{\mu}`$ denote retrieval from trajectory memory under the
filtering rules and budgets for mode $`\mu`$. Under $`\mathrm{none}`$,
$`R(\tau,M_{k},B)`$ returns up to $`B`$ relevant factual records and
their outcomes without synthesis or success-only filtering. The
$`\mathrm{imitation}`$ and $`\mathrm{strategic}`$ modes select up to the
top-$`B`$ successes ($`y=1`$), whereas $`\mathrm{corrective}`$ selects
up to the top-$`B`$ failures ($`y=0`$) and one contrasting success when
available. Each candidate set is ranked by task similarity after
task-type filtering, with a default budget of $`B=5`$
([Section B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).

#### Mode-selection retrieval (input to the bandit).

The contextual bandit in
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
searches the entire outcome log $`\mathcal{L}_{k}`$ using the same task
embedding and cosine similarity, computing
$`\mathrm{sim}(\tau_{i},\tau)`$ for every entry in a single
matrix–vector product. The top-$`\hat{B}`$ entries, or all entries if
fewer are available, form the local neighborhood
$`\mathcal{N}_{\hat{B}}(\tau)`$ used for the cost-adjusted,
recency-weighted reward estimates in
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").
If average neighborhood similarity falls below $`\rho`$, the bandit
falls back to a global-best policy that ignores the neighborhood; both
$`\rho`$ and $`\hat{B}`$ are reported in
[Section B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").

### B.4 Hyperparameters

[Table 3](#A2.T3 "In B.4 Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
lists the method-level hyperparameters and default settings for
anti-persistence, with sensitivity analyses varying only the specified
parameters. Symbols follow the main text, supplemented by parameters
governing bandit exploration, while
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Experimental Setup Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
reports run-level settings such as iteration counts, episodes per
iteration, and per-step budgets.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  Parameter (symbol) |  Default |  Description |
| *Bandit: mode selection* |  |  |
|  KNN neighborhood size $`\hat{B}`$ |  $`10`$ |  top-$`\hat{B}`$ entries form $`\mathcal{N}_{\hat{B}}(\tau)`$ |
|  UCB coefficient $`c`$ |  $`0.5`$ |  exploration bonus base |
|  Recency decay $`\gamma`$ |  $`0.998`$ |  weight $`w_{i}\propto\gamma^{\,t_{\max}-t_{i}}`$ |
|  KNN trust threshold $`\rho`$ |  $`0.7`$ |  fallback to global-best if $`\overline{\mathrm{sim}}<\rho`$ |
|  Per-mode warmup $`W_{\mathrm{init}}`$ |  $`3`$ |  each mode forced at least $`W_{\mathrm{init}}`$ times before KNN-UCB |
|  Round-robin warmup iterations |  $`3`$ |  first $`3`$ iterations enforce round-robin selection |
|  $`\varepsilon`$-greedy rate $`\varepsilon`$ |  $`0.1`$ |  probability of uniform-random mode selection |
|  Reward clipping range |  $`[-1,1]`$ |  per-task bandit reward clipped to this range |
| *Reward shaping* |  |  |
|  Cost weight $`\lambda`$ |  $`0.05`$ |  $`r=\operatorname{clip}(y-\lambda\kappa,-1,1)`$ |
| *Trajectory retrieval (input to $`\phi`$)* |  |  |
|  Success top-$`k`$ ($`B`$) |  $`5`$ |  success trajectories retrieved per call |
|  Failure top-$`k`$ ($`B`$) |  $`5`$ |  failure trajectories (corrective mode only) |
|  Contrasting success top-$`k`$ |  $`1`$ |  success reference for corrective mode |
|  Task-type filter |  on |  retrieval restricted to the current task type |
| *LLM calls* |  |  |
|  Synthesis max tokens |  $`1024`$ |  for $`\phi`$ in imitation, strategic, and corrective |
|  Agent max tokens |  $`1024`$ |  per action / step |
| *Embedding* |  |  |
|  Embedding model |  Qwen3-Embedding-8B |  one call per task; see [Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Retrieval Similarity ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents") |
|  Init-observation prefix length |  $`500`$ chars |  characters of obs concatenated into embed_text |

Table 3: Method hyperparameters and default values. Sensitivity analyses
vary the specified parameters.

The following notes explain the design choices underlying the numerical
defaults.

Round-robin and $`\varepsilon`$-greedy as safeguards. The first three
experimental iterations use round-robin selection to provide initial
mode coverage, subject to the logging exclusions in
[Section B.5](#A2.SS5 "B.5 Outcome-Log Schema and Update Protocol ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").
After warmup, an $`\varepsilon`$-greedy rate of $`0.1`$ maintains
exploration by giving every mode a nonzero chance of selection,
complementing the initial coverage provided by round-robin selection.

KNN trust threshold $`\rho=0.7`$. When the average cosine similarity
within $`\mathcal{N}_{\hat{B}}(\tau)`$ falls below $`\rho`$, the bandit
switches to its global-best fallback, reducing reliance on weak local
matches without guaranteeing accurate global estimates. We set $`\rho`$
to $`0.7`$ using a small validation set and perform no further tuning.

Reward clipping. Per-task bandit rewards
$`r=\operatorname{clip}(y-\lambda\kappa,-1,1)`$ are recorded in the
outcome log $`\mathcal{L}_{k}`$ using the realized synthesis-call count
$`\kappa`$, which is zero when synthesis is skipped. Although the
defaults ($`y\in\{0,1\}`$, $`\lambda=0.05`$, $`\kappa\in\{0,1\}`$)
already produce rewards within this range, clipping accommodates
potential changes in the reward or cost scale.

### B.5 Outcome-Log Schema and Update Protocol

The outcome log $`\mathcal{L}_{k}`$ introduced in
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
records observed mode choices and outcomes without storing synthesized
abstractions. Its schema and update protocol are specified below;
because the recorded outcomes inform later mode selection, this factual
log still permits feedback across tasks.

#### Record schema.

Each entry of $`\mathcal{L}_{k}`$ is a tuple of seven fields:

- •
  embedding (list\[float\]): the task embedding $`\mathbf{e}_{\tau}`$
  from
  [Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Retrieval Similarity ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents"),
  used by the bandit’s KNN lookup;
- •
  mode (str): one of
  $`\{\mathrm{none},\mathrm{imitation},\mathrm{strategic},\mathrm{corrective}\}`$;
- •
  reward (float, clipped to $`[-1,1]`$): the cost-adjusted bandit reward
  $`r=\operatorname{clip}(y-\lambda\kappa,-1,1)`$;
- •
  raw_success (bool): the binary task outcome $`y`$, independent of
  $`\lambda`$;
- •
  task_type (str): the task family (e.g., alfworld);
- •
  task_id (int): the index of $`\tau`$ in its benchmark task pool;
- •
  instruction (str, truncated to $`\leq 500`$ characters): the task
  instruction text, retained for stratified analysis and debugging.

#### Storage format.

$`\mathcal{L}_{k}`$ is stored as a single append-only JSONL file with
one record per line, without rewriting, compaction, or deletion of
entries. The example below displays one record with line breaks and
abbreviated embedding values for readability:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Update protocol.

After each training-task attempt, the agent appends one record to
$`\mathcal{L}_{k}`$, subject to three skip rules:

1.  1.
    *The initial task update $`k=0`$ is excluded.* At $`k=0`$,
    trajectory memory $`M_{k}`$ is empty and all modes reduce to
    baseline behavior. Logging this outcome would attribute baseline
    noise to the selected mode.
2.  2.
    *Embedding failures are excluded.* If the embedding API call for
    $`\tau`$ fails, the record cannot enter KNN retrieval and is
    dropped.
3.  3.
    *Infrastructure failures are excluded.* Records from abnormal
    terminations, such as environment exceptions, are skipped because
    their outcomes cannot be attributed to the selected mode.

These rules exclude attempts with empty initial memory, missing
embeddings, or infrastructure failures, but do not remove task-selection
effects or other confounding from the remaining observations.

#### Read protocol.

On startup, the JSONL file is streamed to reload $`\mathcal{L}_{k}`$ in
file order, using the following conventions for timestamp assignment and
corrupted records.

Relative timestamps. Logical timestamps $`t_{i}`$ follow log order
without being stored in the file, and each appended entry receives a
timestamp $`t_{\mathrm{new}}`$ later than those of existing entries.
Reloading assigns consecutive integer ranks that preserve order while
ignoring elapsed time and previous timestamp spacing. For a fixed loaded
log, anchoring decay at the latest neighborhood timestamp $`t_{\max}`$
rather than the current update index rescales every weight by the same
positive factor, leaving normalized reward estimates unchanged.

Tolerance to corrupted lines. Malformed lines, such as those caused by
interrupted writes, are skipped with a logged warning while loading
continues, preventing a single corrupted record from invalidating the
log.

## Appendix D Experimental Setup Details

This appendix details the task splits, training and evaluation protocol,
backbone configurations, and AutoRefine implementation used in the
experiments. All memory and controller updates use training experience;
held-out outcomes remain separate from the update process.

### D.1 Per-Benchmark Task Counts and Partitioning

For each benchmark, a fixed *training set* supplies interaction
experience for memory and controller-state updates with backbone
parameters held fixed, while a separate fixed *held-out set* is reserved
for evaluation. Where available, we adopt community-standard splits from
prior work \[[18](#bib.bib2), [35](#bib.bib3), [3](#bib.bib13),
[5](#bib.bib16)\], with task counts reported in
[Table 4](#A4.T4 "In D.1 Per-Benchmark Task Counts and Partitioning ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
and the per-iteration sampling procedure described below.

| Benchmark | Training tasks | Held-out tasks |  Evaluation set |
|----|----|----|----|
| ALFWorld | $`180`$ | $`134`$ |  $`134`$ unseen tasks \[[18](#bib.bib2), [35](#bib.bib3)\] |
| WebShop | $`200`$ | $`100`$ |  $`100`$ held-out instructions |
| ScienceWorld | $`150`$ | $`60`$ |  $`2`$ held-out instances per task type |

Table 4: Per-benchmark training and held-out task counts used in this
study.

#### ALFWorld.

ALFWorld \[[19](#bib.bib33)\] provides $`3{,}553`$ training games and
$`134`$ unseen evaluation games across six categories: Pick & Place,
Examine in Light, Clean & Place, Heat & Place, Cool & Place, and Pick
Two & Place. We adopt the $`134`$-task held-out split used in prior work
\[[18](#bib.bib2), [35](#bib.bib3)\] and draw $`30`$ tasks per category
to obtain a balanced training set of $`180`$ tasks. Although AutoManual
\[[3](#bib.bib13)\] uses smaller per-category splits, our setup follows
the larger Reflexion/ExpeL evaluation protocol while keeping the
training set manageable.

#### WebShop.

WebShop \[[30](#bib.bib34)\] provides $`12{,}087`$ crowd-sourced
shopping instructions paired with target product descriptions and
structured attributes. We use a fixed $`100`$-instruction held-out set.
This evaluation size differs from the original benchmark’s
$`500`$-instruction test split \[[30](#bib.bib34)\]. We uniformly sample
$`200`$ training instructions from the remaining $`11{,}987`$ using a
fixed random seed to ensure a common training stream across methods.

#### ScienceWorld.

ScienceWorld \[[24](#bib.bib35)\] provides $`30`$ task types in
elementary science, including thermodynamics, electricity, and biology,
with multiple parameterized variations of each type. We construct a
stratified partition by randomly selecting $`N_{\mathrm{train}}=5`$
training instances and $`N_{\mathrm{held}}=2`$ nonoverlapping held-out
instances for each of the $`30`$ types. The resulting $`150`$ training
tasks and $`60`$ held-out tasks cover every task type, enabling
evaluation on unseen variations within each type. Sampling once with a
fixed random seed gives all methods the same partition, supporting
controlled comparisons within this paper despite the difference from
prior protocols.

#### Per-iteration training subset.

At each experimental iteration $`\ell`$, we sample
$`N_{\mathrm{train/iter}}=50`$ training tasks uniformly without
replacement and attempt them sequentially in an order determined by a
fixed random seed. These episodes alone may update each method’s memory
and related state according to its update procedure, yielding $`500`$
training episodes per benchmark across $`K=10`$ iterations. All methods
receive the same sample at iteration $`\ell`$, controlling for
training-task composition in comparisons of memory designs.

After each iteration’s training updates, each method is evaluated on the
full held-out set with memory and related state frozen. Held-out
episodes use a separate log that is never carried forward and cannot
update trajectory or abstraction memory, $`\mathcal{L}_{k}`$, retrieval
metadata, maintenance scores, the skill evolver, or pruning. Each
episode permits up to $`50`$ environment steps, with attempts exceeding
this budget terminated as failures ($`y=0`$).

### D.2 Backbone Configurations

We evaluate three open-weight backbones from distinct model
families—Llama-4-Scout, Qwen3-Coder-Next, and Gemma-4-31B-it—running
locally through OpenAI-compatible inference endpoints with the hardware
and context lengths in
[Table 5](#A4.T5 "In D.2 Backbone Configurations ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").
All methods share the same agent prompt and per-step output budget to
control these factors when comparing memory configurations.

| Model | Inference hardware | Context length |
|----|----|----|
| Llama-4-Scout \[[10](#bib.bib29)\] | $`2\times`$ NVIDIA H100 | 64K |
| Qwen3-Coder-Next \[[2](#bib.bib30)\] | $`4\times`$ NVIDIA H100 | 256K |
| Gemma-4-31B-it \[[8](#bib.bib32)\] | $`4\times`$ NVIDIA L40S | 256K |

Table 5: Backbone configurations.

#### Embedding model.

Qwen3-Embedding-8B \[[34](#bib.bib31)\] produces task embeddings for
trajectory retrieval
([Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Retrieval Similarity ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents"))
and KNN lookup through an OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint on the
same cluster. Anti-persistence makes one embedding call per task using
the same encoder with every backbone, ensuring a common embedding
representation for outcome-log similarity comparisons across
configurations.

### D.3 AutoRefine Baseline Implementation

Our AutoRefine baseline adapts the maintenance procedure of [Qiu et al.
\[15\]](#bib.bib14), using the same retrieval and per-iteration episode
budgets as the other methods
([Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
The five components below include utility scoring, retrieval, pruning,
synthesis, and the update loop. This baseline therefore differs from
abstraction memory in more than maintenance alone. Its results are
reported in
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.2 Algorithm Design ‣ 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
and
[Figure 7](#S4.F7 "In 4.3 Dynamics Across Self-Improvement Rounds ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").

#### (i) Per-skill utility score.

For each stored skill $`s`$, the metadata triple
$`(n^{\mathrm{inj}}_{s},\,n^{\mathrm{succ}}_{s},\,t^{\mathrm{create}}_{s})`$
records its prompt-inclusion count, the number of successful episodes
among those inclusions, and its creation iteration. We define skill
utility as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{score}(s)\;=\;\underbrace{\frac{n^{\mathrm{succ}}_{s}}{n^{\mathrm{inj}}_{s}+\varepsilon}}_{\text{effectiveness}}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{\log\!\big(1+n^{\mathrm{inj}}_{s}\big)}_{\text{frequency}},
``` |  | (4) |

with $`\varepsilon=10^{-3}`$, so the frequency factor discounts skills
supported by only one or two retrievals, while skills that have never
appeared in a successful episode receive zero. This metadata is stored
in a JSON file alongside the skill files.

#### (ii) Multi-query retrieval with similarity floor and MMR diversification.

For each episode, the backbone rewrites the task description into three
queries emphasizing *strategy*, *pitfall*, and *actions*, which join the
original description to form four query strings. Each query is embedded
with Qwen3-Embedding-8B
([Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Retrieval Similarity ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
and a candidate skill’s relevance is its maximum cosine similarity
across the queries. After discarding candidates below the similarity
threshold of $`0.30`$, we re-rank the remainder using Maximal Marginal
Relevance with diversity weight $`\lambda_{\mathrm{MMR}}=0.7`$,
selecting at each step the skill that maximizes

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\lambda_{\mathrm{MMR}}\,\mathrm{rel}(s)\;-\;(1-\lambda_{\mathrm{MMR}})\,\max_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{sel}}}\,\mathrm{sim}(s,s^{\prime}),
``` |  | (5) |

and concatenating the top $`5`$ entries into the prompt. Candidates are
drawn from the general-skill set, the common-mistakes set, and the
benchmark’s task-type-specific skill set.

#### (iii) Periodic percentile pruning.

Every two iterations (at $`\ell=2,4,\ldots,K`$), we prune the bottom
$`20\%`$ of eligible skills by utility score, with eligibility
restricted to *$`n^{\mathrm{inj}}_{s}\geq 3`$* to protect skills with
little retrieval history. A single transaction removes the selected
entries from the in-memory dictionary, on-disk skill files, and metadata
file while invalidating their embedding caches.

#### (iv) Contrastive skill evolver.

After each iteration, a single contrastive prompt extracts new skills
from at most four failure episodes and four sampled success episodes,
using a benchmark-specific system preamble for ALFWorld, WebShop, or
ScienceWorld. Each generated skill must include a Why it works section
that contrasts the success and failure evidence. The synthesizer’s
output is decoded as a JSON array through a four-stage fallback parser
comprising direct parsing, fenced-block stripping, extraction of the
last bracketed array, and per-object scanning; skills with non-slug
names are renamed dyn-$`N`$, using the smallest $`N`$ above the maximum
existing index. This single-call evolver replaces the original
AutoRefine release’s two-call procedure for reflecting on failures and
extracting experience from successes, placing both forms of evidence in
the shared context required by the contrastive prompt.

#### (v) Per-iteration update loop.

Each AutoRefine iteration $`\ell`$ runs the following loop:

1.  1.
    Reset the training retrieval log for the current iteration.
2.  2.
    Run the training episodes for iteration $`\ell`$, invoking the
    multi-query retrieval procedure in step (ii) for each episode.
3.  3.
    Update metadata from the training retrieval log. For each skill
    included in an episode’s prompt, set
    $`n^{\mathrm{inj}}_{s}\mathrel{+}=1`$ and, if that episode
    succeeded, $`n^{\mathrm{succ}}_{s}\mathrel{+}=1`$.
4.  4.
    Run the contrastive evolver in step (iv) using only training
    outcomes. Add the new skills to the store and set
    $`t^{\mathrm{create}}_{s}=\ell`$.
5.  5.
    If $`\ell>0`$ and $`\ell`$ is even, run percentile pruning (step
    (iii)) and write a metadata checkpoint.
6.  6.
    Freeze the resulting state and evaluate on the full held-out set.
    Held-out episodes may retrieve skills, but a separate log records
    their retrievals and outcomes. These records do not update skill
    files, metadata, the evolver, or pruning.

The training retrieval log identifies each injection by the tuple (task
type, task description, initial observation), and Step (3) credits a
successful retrieval only when the skill appeared in that episode’s
prompt. Successes achieved without retrieving the skill therefore do not
increase its utility score.

The main text reports per-iteration performance on Llama-4-Scout and

and aggregate per-task LLM-call cost

This appendix extends that evaluation with success-rate and
trajectory-length curves for Gemma-4-31B-it
([Section E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Per-Iteration Curves on Gemma-4-31B-it ‣ Appendix E Extended Cross-Backbone Results ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
a cost breakdown for every $`(\text{backbone}\times\text{benchmark})`$

and an analysis of whether descendants with flagged parents are more
likely to be flagged themselves
([Section E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Provenance Associations and Operational Bias Flags ‣ Appendix E Extended Cross-Backbone Results ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
The latter describes historical associations relevant to the proposed
error-reproduction pathway.
````
