````math
### E.3 Provenance Associations and Operational Bias Flags

We describe an audit of parent–descendant associations relevant to the
pathway in
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Reproduction Dynamics in Abstraction Memory ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents"),
combining historical exposure records with outcome-based flags assigned
after evaluation. The equations below specify the intended quantities
and their data requirements, while
[Figure 11](#A5.F11 "In Results and scope. ‣ E.3 Provenance Associations and Operational Bias Flags ‣ Appendix E Extended Cross-Backbone Results ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
retains the supplied aggregates, which have not been recomputed for this
revision or verified against event-level provenance and
labeling-eligibility logs. The audit therefore remains descriptive and
cannot establish a causal reproduction effect or a long-run growth
coefficient.

#### Descendant tracking.

For a candidate $`s=\phi(H)`$, its historical parent set is

|     |                            |     |
|-----|----------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       P(s)=\bigcup_{m\in H}P(m),
       ```                         |     |

where $`P(m)`$ records the persistent abstractions present in the
context when execution record $`m`$ was generated, retaining their
historical identifiers even after the corresponding objects leave the
current store $`S_{k}`$. Parent sets are recorded as analysis metadata
when a candidate is created, without retroactively modifying the agent’s
memory. They document exposure and data lineage but do not establish
that an abstraction caused a particular action or error.

#### Operational labeling.

For each historically stored abstraction, the audit compares held-out
episodes that retrieved it with episodes that did not. Let
$`n_{s}^{+},n_{s}^{-}`$ and $`\bar{y}_{s}^{+},\bar{y}_{s}^{-}`$ denote
the respective episode counts and mean success rates. Define the set of
abstractions eligible for labeling as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathrm{lab}}=\{s:n_{s}^{+}\geq n_{\min},\ n_{s}^{-}>0\}.
``` |  |

For $`s`$ in this set, assign

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{b}(s)=\mathbf{1}\{\bar{y}_{s}^{-}-\bar{y}_{s}^{+}\geq\delta\},\qquad n_{\min}=3,\quad\delta=0.05,
``` |  |

and let
$`\widehat{\mathcal{B}}=\{s\in\widehat{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathrm{lab}}:\widehat{b}(s)=1\}`$.
Abstractions outside the eligible set remain unclassified throughout the
audit, and both comparison groups must exist to avoid assigning labels
from undefined means. These unadjusted operational flags instantiate
[Definition 1](#Thmdefinition1 "Definition 1 (Operational bias labels). ‣ A.1 Operational Bias Labels and Historical Provenance ‣ Appendix A Reproduction Dynamics in Abstraction Memory ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
without estimating causal harm, since retrieval may, for example,
concentrate certain abstractions on more difficult tasks.

The audit uses held-out logs collected with memory and related state
frozen, with labels and provenance analyses computed after the runs so
that they cannot influence memory updates, maintenance scores, pruning,
or subsequent behavior. Comparisons between the groups below require a
common evaluation protocol and common audit thresholds.

#### Empirical conditional rates.

Let $`\mathcal{V}`$ contain historically stored descendants that satisfy
the labeling-eligibility conditions above and have a recorded historical
parent set. Define
$`F(s)=\mathbf{1}\{P(s)\cap\widehat{\mathcal{B}}\neq\emptyset\}`$. The
intended descriptive group rates are

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{\alpha}_{\mathrm{emp}}=\frac{\sum_{s\in\mathcal{V}}F(s)\widehat{b}(s)}{\sum_{s\in\mathcal{V}}F(s)},\qquad\widehat{\alpha}_{0}=\frac{\sum_{s\in\mathcal{V}}(1-F(s))\widehat{b}(s)}{\sum_{s\in\mathcal{V}}(1-F(s))},
``` |  |

provided the corresponding denominator is positive, with a zero
denominator leaving the rate undefined. The first group contains
descendants with at least one flagged parent, whereas the second
contains those with none; because the latter may include unclassified
parents or an empty parent set, it does not constitute a group with
verified benign ancestry.

These pooled observational rates describe conditional associations
across the logged states rather than estimating $`\alpha`$ for a single
fixed post-maintenance state. They also condition on prior storage and
labeling eligibility, so they cannot separately identify candidate-level
generation and admission rates. Comparing against
$`\widehat{\alpha}_{0}`$ leaves task difficulty, retrieval selection,
parent-set size, and other potential confounders uncontrolled, while
shared ancestors and evaluation episodes introduce dependence among
observations.

#### Results and scope.

Descendants with at least one flagged parent had a higher flag rate in
most of the six logged settings
([Figure 11](#A5.F11 "In Results and scope. ‣ E.3 Provenance Associations and Operational Bias Flags ‣ Appendix E Extended Cross-Backbone Results ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
with the largest reported gap,
$`\widehat{\alpha}_{\mathrm{emp}}-\widehat{\alpha}_{0}=+0.55`$,
occurring on Llama-4-Scout with ALFWorld. This association is consistent
with the proposed pathway but identifies neither inherited error content
nor a causal effect of parent exposure. The absence of group counts,
labeling coverage, and an uncertainty-estimation procedure limits
statistical interpretation of the aggregates, which cannot establish a
causal amplification factor, a retention probability, or a threshold for
long-run instability.

Figure 10: Observational flagged-descendant rates across six settings.
Groups have at least one flagged parent or no flagged parent; absence of
a flag does not establish benign ancestry. The largest reported rate gap
is $`+0.55`$. Error bars are retained as reported, but their estimation
procedure is unavailable with the aggregate data.

(b) WebShop ($`K=10`$).

## Appendix F Additional Controlled and Statistical Analyses

Three additional analyses examine the immediate effect of supplied skill
content
([Figure 11(a)](#A5.F11.sf1 "In Figure 11 ‣ Results and scope. ‣ E.3 Provenance Associations and Operational Bias Flags ‣ Appendix E Extended Cross-Backbone Results ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
selective retention of filtered skills
([Figure 11(b)](#A5.F11.sf2 "In Figure 11 ‣ Results and scope. ‣ E.3 Provenance Associations and Operational Bias Flags ‣ Appendix E Extended Cross-Backbone Results ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
and consistency of performance differences across the nine main
evaluation settings
([Table 7](#A6.T7 "In F.3 Setting-Level Consistency Across the Main Evaluation Grid ‣ Appendix F Additional Controlled and Statistical Analyses ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
The two controlled analyses report aggregate success rates, with
task-level and seed-level observations unavailable for estimating
uncertainty.

### F.1 Effects of Skill Content on AppWorld

We tested the immediate effect of skill content on 30 randomly selected
AppWorld tasks \[[22](#bib.bib36)\], using matched pairs of reusable
skills constructed by GPT-5.5 before evaluation. Each pair shared the
same intended scope but contained a useful version with a correct
procedural rule and a toxic version with an incorrect rule; these labels
denote constructed conditions rather than the outcome-based flags in
[Section E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Provenance Associations and Operational Bias Flags ‣ Appendix E Extended Cross-Backbone Results ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").
With the skill libraries frozen, Qwen3-Coder-Next attempted the same
tasks under three conditions: no supplied skills, useful skills, and
toxic skills.

With the acting model, task set, and intended skill scope held fixed,
aggregate success was $`23.0\%`$ without supplied skills, $`40.0\%`$
with useful skills, and $`20.0\%`$ with toxic skills
([Figure 11(a)](#A5.F11.sf1 "In Figure 11 ‣ Results and scope. ‣ E.3 Provenance Associations and Operational Bias Flags ‣ Appendix E Extended Cross-Backbone Results ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
These results characterize the immediate effects of supplied abstraction
content on performance without establishing whether the resulting
trajectories generate biased descendants or sustain error reproduction
across iterations.

### F.2 Selective Skill Retention on WebShop

We examined selective skill retention on WebShop with Qwen3-Coder-Next
under two configurations: GPT-5.5 assessed each newly generated skill
before admission to persistent abstraction memory in the first, while
the selected skills were added to anti-persistence as a frozen
persistent-memory layer in the second.

Within this auxiliary evaluation, filtering increased the final success
rate of abstraction memory from $`38.7\%`$ to $`46.0\%`$, whereas adding
the frozen layer to anti-persistence reduced its final success rate from
$`56.0\%`$ to $`44.0\%`$
([Figure 11(b)](#A5.F11.sf2 "In Figure 11 ‣ Results and scope. ‣ E.3 Provenance Associations and Operational Bias Flags ‣ Appendix E Extended Cross-Backbone Results ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).

The tested filter and retention protocol thus improved the
abstraction-memory baseline but reduced performance when the filtered
skills were added to anti-persistence. Because the added layer remained
frozen, its performance effect does not establish descendant generation
or error reproduction across iterations.

### F.3 Setting-Level Consistency Across the Main Evaluation Grid

To assess consistency across the nine fixed
$`(\text{backbone}\times\text{benchmark})`$ settings in
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.2 Algorithm Design ‣ 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents"),
we computed the difference between anti-persistence and each baseline
within every setting. We then summarized these paired differences by
their equally weighted mean in percentage points and the number of
settings with a positive difference.

For an exploratory statistical summary, we computed nominal 95%
$`t`$-intervals, two-sided paired $`t`$-tests, and exact two-sided
Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, applying Holm correction separately to the
seven baseline comparisons within each test family while leaving the
intervals unadjusted. All calculations used the one-decimal cell means
in
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.2 Algorithm Design ‣ 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents"),
with NumPy 2.5.0 and SciPy 1.18.1.

[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.2 Algorithm Design ‣ 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").
$`\Delta`$ denotes anti-persistence minus the named baseline, measured
in percentage points. CIs are nominal, unadjusted 95% $`t`$-intervals,
and all tests are two-sided. Holm correction covers the seven baseline
comparisons within each test family. Shared backbones and benchmarks
limit the inferential interpretation of these statistics.

Anti-persistence achieved higher success in all nine settings against
five baselines and in eight settings against Reflexion and joint memory
([Table 7](#A6.T7 "In F.3 Setting-Level Consistency Across the Main Evaluation Grid ‣ Appendix F Additional Controlled and Statistical Analyses ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
with mean differences ranging from $`+6.4`$ to $`+19.2`$ percentage
points. The direction of its advantage was therefore consistent across
most or all settings for each baseline.

Although all seven Holm-adjusted $`p`$-values were below $`0.05`$ in
each test family, the shared backbones and benchmarks limit the
treatment of the nine settings as independent observations. Holm
correction addresses multiple comparisons without resolving this
dependence, so the nominal intervals and $`p`$-values remain exploratory
summaries rather than evidence for population-level significance. They
neither quantify seed-level uncertainty within settings nor justify
extrapolation to untested models and benchmarks.

## Appendix G Sensitivity and Robustness Studies

We examine sensitivity to the two retrieval budgets introduced in
[Section B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents"):
the trajectory budget $`B`$, which controls the records supplied for
direct reuse or synthesis
([Section G.1](#A7.SS1 "G.1 Trajectory Retrieval Budget 𝐵 Sensitivity ‣ Appendix G Sensitivity and Robustness Studies ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")),
and the outcome-log budget $`\hat{B}`$, which controls the records used
for mode selection
([Section G.2](#A7.SS2 "G.2 Outcome-Log Retrieval Budget 𝐵̂ Sensitivity ‣ Appendix G Sensitivity and Robustness Studies ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).

### G.1 Trajectory Retrieval Budget $`B`$ Sensitivity

The base trajectory retrieval budget $`B`$ limits the records retrieved
under the mode-specific rules
([Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Retrieval Similarity ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")):
up to $`B`$ records for direct reuse under $`\mathrm{none}`$, up to
$`B`$ successes for imitation and strategic synthesis, or up to $`B`$
failures and one optional success for corrective synthesis. To assess
the effect of supplying fewer or more records as context, we evaluate
$`B\in\{1,5,10\}`$ on Qwen3-Coder-Next with ALFWorld and WebShop, using
three seeds per setting.

Observations.
[Figure 12(a)](#A7.F12.sf1 "In Figure 12 ‣ G.1 Trajectory Retrieval Budget 𝐵 Sensitivity ‣ Appendix G Sensitivity and Robustness Studies ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
shows that both tested alternatives to the default retrieval budget
yielded lower success rates.

(i) The smallest retrieval budget underperformed. At $`B=1`$, direct
reuse receives at most one record; synthesis receives at most one
success for imitation or strategic mode, or one failure and an optional
success for corrective mode. The resulting success rates of $`86.0\%`$
on ALFWorld and $`46.0\%`$ on WebShop were below the default, consistent
with greater sensitivity to individual examples when only a few records
are available.

(ii) The largest retrieval budget also underperformed. At $`B=10`$,
success rates were $`91.3\%`$ on ALFWorld and $`48.7\%`$ on WebShop,
again below the default. Adding more weakly related trajectories may
dilute the useful context for direct reuse or synthesis, although this
sweep does not isolate that explanation.

(iii) The default setting $`B=5`$ performed best among the tested
values. The default budget gave the highest observed success rates on
both benchmarks, favoring an intermediate tested value as in the
recency-decay analysis
([Figure 7](#S4.F7 "In 4.3 Dynamics Across Self-Improvement Rounds ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
This pattern is consistent with a trade-off between local relevance and
coverage of retrieved experience.

(a) Trajectory retrieval budget $`B`$. The default $`B=5`$ yields the
highest success rate among the tested values.

(b) Outcome-log retrieval budget $`\hat{B}`$. The default $`\hat{B}=10`$
yields the highest success rate among the tested values.

Figure 12: Sensitivity to trajectory retrieval budget $`B`$ and
outcome-log retrieval budget $`\hat{B}`$ on Qwen3-Coder-Next. Bars show
means over $`3`$ seeds; error bars show standard deviations across
seeds.

### G.2 Outcome-Log Retrieval Budget $`\hat{B}`$ Sensitivity

The outcome-log retrieval budget $`\hat{B}`$ limits the size of the
bandit’s local neighborhood and thus the number of nearby observations
available for mode selection
([Section B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Method Details ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
We evaluate $`\hat{B}\in\{3,5,20\}`$ on Qwen3-Coder-Next with ALFWorld
and WebShop, using three seeds per setting, and compare these
alternatives with the default $`\hat{B}=10`$ configuration in
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.2 Algorithm Design ‣ 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents").

Observations.
[Figure 12(b)](#A7.F12.sf2 "In Figure 12 ‣ G.1 Trajectory Retrieval Budget 𝐵 Sensitivity ‣ Appendix G Sensitivity and Robustness Studies ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
shows the same qualitative pattern as the trajectory-budget sweep, with
the default neighborhood size outperforming both smaller and larger
tested values.

(i) Smaller neighborhoods yielded lower success rates. With only a few
observations available for local reward estimation at $`\hat{B}=3`$,
held-out success was $`90.0\%`$ on ALFWorld and $`45.3\%`$ on WebShop.
Increasing the neighborhood to $`\hat{B}=5`$ improved these rates to
$`92.0\%`$ and $`46.7\%`$, respectively, although both remained below
the default, potentially reflecting greater sensitivity to individual
outcomes in small neighborhoods.

(ii) The largest neighborhood also underperformed. At $`\hat{B}=20`$,
success rates were $`92.0\%`$ on ALFWorld and $`50.0\%`$ on WebShop,
again below the default. Including more weakly related tasks may reduce
the relevance of local reward estimates, although the sweep does not
directly test this explanation.

(iii) The default setting $`\hat{B}=10`$ performed best among the tested
values. The default neighborhood size gave the highest observed success
rates on both benchmarks, complementing the trajectory-budget sweep in
[Section G.1](#A7.SS1 "G.1 Trajectory Retrieval Budget 𝐵 Sensitivity ‣ Appendix G Sensitivity and Robustness Studies ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")
and remaining consistent with a trade-off between local relevance and
evidence coverage. These results support the default budgets within the
tested ranges and settings without establishing a general optimum.

## Appendix H Limitations

Anti-persistence prevents direct reuse of stored abstractions, but
temporary guidance can still influence later synthesis through
trajectories. Its performance also depends on retrieval quality and
experience coverage. Our main iterative experiments cover three
text-based benchmarks with fixed backbones and a fixed improvement
procedure; broader generalization and longer-term gains remain untested.
The two controlled auxiliary analyses lack task-level and seed-level
uncertainty estimates, while the setting-level statistics remain
exploratory
([Appendix F](#A6 "Appendix F Additional Controlled and Statistical Analyses ‣ More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents")).
Discarding abstractions also forgoes the benefits of reusing reliable
knowledge across tasks. Future work could examine when external
verification or uncertainty estimates justify selective persistence.
````
